claims.text: Reactive melt/inoculation with controlled oxygen addition and subsequent heat treatment will produce oxide dispersoids in an Nb-Mo-Ta-Ti refractory high-entropy alloy.
The proposed processing will yield a uniform distribution of oxide dispersoids throughout the alloy matrix.
The resulting oxide dispersoids will be approximately 10–20 nm in diameter.
A short heat treatment at 1100–1200 °C followed by rapid quenching will control oxide precipitation and dispersion.
The oxide dispersoids will obstruct dislocation motion through Orowan looping.
The oxide dispersoids will limit grain-boundary sliding.
The nanoscale oxide dispersoids will stabilize microstructural features at high temperature.
The dispersoid-modified alloy will exhibit at least a 25% improvement in yield strength at approximately 1000 °C relative to the alloy without dispersoids.
The dispersoid-modified alloy will exhibit at least a 25% improvement in creep resistance at approximately 1000 °C relative to the alloy without dispersoids.
The high-temperature improvement will hold under creep or stress-rupture loading.
The dispersoid-modified alloy will retain room-temperature ductility comparable to that of the baseline alloy.
The oxide-dispersoid intervention will cause only a minimal increase in alloy density.
The modified alloy will retain a low overall density.
A controlled nanoscale particle size and volume fraction will prevent deterioration of room-temperature ductility.
The predicted performance gains depend critically on maintaining a uniform dispersoid distribution.
Significant particle coarsening or inhomogeneity during prolonged high-temperature exposure could compromise the mechanical benefits.
